justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across time horizons, starting near 91.5 for the one-day horizon and rising gradually to 93.5 at one month. This pattern is consistent with a mean-reverting or slowly trending asset that I assessed to be trading slightly below some fundamental or technical anchor level at the time of the forecast. The one-day estimate is anchored closely to the prevailing price, with very little expected drift, since markets tend to be relatively efficient over short windows. The one-week and one-month estimates incorporate a small positive drift assumption, possibly reflecting momentum, a growth trend, or an expectation that any short-term undervaluation would partially correct over time.

Confidence interval widths expand substantially as the horizon lengthens, which is standard for probabilistic price forecasts. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 8 points, reflecting typical intraday-to-next-day volatility. By one week, it widens to 16 points, and at one month it reaches 36 points. These widths are driven by realized or implied volatility estimates for the underlying asset, compounding uncertainty over time roughly in proportion to the square root of the time horizon. Macroeconomic data releases, earnings announcements, or policy decisions scheduled within the forecast window would also have contributed to widening intervals at longer horizons.

Several risks could push outcomes outside the stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected negative shock — such as a surprise central bank tightening, geopolitical escalation, or a disappointing earnings or economic report — could push prices well below the lower bound, particularly at the one-month horizon. Liquidity crises or sudden shifts in market sentiment can produce fat-tailed moves that probabilistic models based on historical volatility tend to underestimate. On the upside, a strong positive catalyst such as better-than-expected economic data, a policy pivot, or a short squeeze could drive prices above the upper bound. The one-month interval of 76 to 112 is wide enough to capture most plausible scenarios, but truly extreme tail events — a systemic financial disruption or a major geopolitical surprise — remain outside even that range.
